name: Quantitative evaluation, version 3
models: Reported, as of Nov 2026: SIG's Quantitative Evaluation. Seventeen questions in 60 minutes with a calculator, rising from quick expected values to multi-stage Bayes and ruin.
description: This is the reported format of SIG's Quantitative Evaluation, as candidates described it by Nov 2026. You have 17 questions in 60 minutes. A calculator is allowed, but the app has none, so have a basic one ready. The questions start with quick expected values and end with multi-stage Bayes and gambler's ruin. Some take a choice, others a number to three decimal places. A wrong answer scores 0, and you may change answers until you submit. Other reports give 16 questions in 20 minutes; this mock follows the longer one. This is version 3 of 3.

items.title: Doubles pay double
items.question: You roll two fair dice and are paid the total in pounds. If the dice show a double, the payout is doubled. What is a fair price to play once?

options.why: You left out the doubling. A double pays its total once more.
You doubled every roll. Only doubles, one roll in six, are doubled.
You gave doubles a chance of $\tfrac{1}{36}$. There are six doubles, so the chance is $\tfrac16$.

feedback.correct: The total averages £7, and doubles add their total again: $7 + \tfrac{42}{36} \approx 8.17$.
feedback.generic: Write the payout as the total, plus the total again on a double, and average each part.

explain.text: The payout is the total $S$, plus $S$ again on a double. So $E = 7 + \tfrac{2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12}{36} = 7 + \tfrac{42}{36} = \tfrac{49}{6} \approx 8.17$. Check: doubles come one time in 6 and average a total of 7, so the extra is $\tfrac16 \times 7$.

items.title: Back to level
items.question: You toss a fair coin 6 times, scoring +1 for each head and −1 for each tail. What is the expected number of tosses after which your running score is exactly 0?

options.why: You gave each even toss a chance of a half. Level after $2k$ tosses needs exactly $k$ heads.
You counted toss 2 only. The score can also be level after tosses 4 and 6.
You counted toss 6 only. Add the chances after tosses 2 and 4.

feedback.correct: The score is level after tosses 2, 4 and 6 with chances $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac38$ and $\tfrac{5}{16}$, which add to $\tfrac{19}{16} \approx 1.19$.
feedback.generic: Give each toss an indicator for a level score. Only even tosses can be level.

explain.text: After $2k$ tosses the score is 0 with chance $\binom{2k}{k} / 4^k$: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac38$ and $\tfrac{5}{16}$. Linearity adds them: $\tfrac{8 + 6 + 5}{16} = \tfrac{19}{16} \approx 1.19$. Check: the 64 sequences hold 76 level points in all, and $\tfrac{76}{64} = \tfrac{19}{16}$.

items.title: Odds of 4 to 1
items.question: You stake £10 on a fair die showing a six, at odds of 4 to 1. A six returns your £10 plus £40, and any other face loses the £10. What is your expected profit?

options.why: You counted the win and not the loss. Five faces in six lose the £10.
You took the £40 as the whole return. The stake comes back on top of it.
You counted the loss and not the win. A six gains £40.

feedback.generic: Write the two outcomes as profits, +£40 and −£10, then weight them.

explain.text: A six gains £40 and any other face loses £10, so $E = \tfrac16 \times 40 - \tfrac56 \times 10 = -\tfrac{10}{6} \approx -1.67$ pounds. Check: 6 bets stake £60 and on average return £50, so each loses £1.67.

items.title: Pairs out of order
items.question: Six orders with different prices arrive in a random order. A pair of orders is out of order when the higher price arrives first. What is the expected number of pairs out of order?

options.why: You counted every pair. Each is out of order only half the time.
You checked only neighbouring arrivals. Any two orders form a pair.
You gave each order a half. Count pairs of orders instead.

feedback.correct: There are $\binom62 = 15$ pairs, each out of order with chance $\tfrac12$, so 7.5.
feedback.generic: Give every pair of orders an indicator. By symmetry, each pair is equally likely to arrive either way round.

explain.text: Each of the $\binom62 = 15$ pairs arrives higher price first with chance $\tfrac12$, so the expected count is $15 \times \tfrac12 = 7.5$. Check: reversing an arrival order turns $m$ such pairs into $15 - m$, so the average is half of 15.

items.title: Dice for coefficients
items.question: You roll two fair dice and get $B$ and $C$. What is the chance that $x^2 + Bx + C = 0$ has a real root? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: For $B = 1$ to 6, the counts of $C$ with $B^2 \ge 4C$ are 0, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 6: $\tfrac{19}{36} \approx 0.528$.
feedback.generic: A real root needs $B^2 - 4C \ge 0$. For each $B$, count the values of $C$ that pass.

byKey.strict: You left out the double roots, where $B^2 = 4C$. A repeated root is still real.
byKey.no-four: You tested $B^2 \ge C$. The discriminant is $B^2 - 4C$.

explain.text: The counts of $C$ with $4C \le B^2$ are 0, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 6 for $B = 1$ to 6. That is 19 of the 36 rolls, $\tfrac{19}{36} \approx 0.528$. Check: the 17 failing rolls are 6 with $B = 1$, 5 with $B = 2$, 4 with $B = 3$ and 2 with $B = 4$.

items.title: The first beats the second
items.question: Three cards are dealt face down from ten cards numbered 1 to 10. You are told the first card is higher than the second. What is the chance the first card is the highest of the three?

options.why: That ignores the news. The first card has already beaten one rival.
You made it an even contest with the third card. Beating the second makes the first card likely to be high.
That is the chance of one full order: first, then second, then third.

feedback.generic: The six orders of the three cards are equally likely. Keep the three where the first beats the second.

explain.text: Of the six equally likely orders, three have the first card above the second. In two of those the first is highest, so the chance is $\tfrac23$. Check: the first card is highest with chance $\tfrac13$, and then it always beats the second, so $\tfrac{1/3}{1/2} = \tfrac23$.

items.title: The third head
items.question: You toss a fair coin until the third head. What is the chance the third head comes on the fifth toss?

options.why: That is exactly three heads in five tosses. The fifth toss must be one of them.
That counts one order only. The first two heads can sit in any 2 of the first 4 tosses.
You left out the fifth toss. It must be a head, which halves the chance.

feedback.correct: Two heads in the first four tosses, $\tfrac{6}{16}$, then a head: $\tfrac{3}{16}$.
feedback.generic: The fifth toss is a head, and the first four hold exactly two heads.

explain.text: The first four tosses must hold exactly two heads, chance $\tfrac{6}{16}$, and the fifth must be a head, chance $\tfrac12$. So the chance is $\tfrac{6}{32} = \tfrac{3}{16}$. Check: of the $\binom53 = 10$ placings of three heads in five tosses, the 6 that end in a head give $\tfrac{6}{32}$.

items.title: Heaviest and lightest
items.question: Ten parcels all weigh different amounts. A balance compares two parcels at a time. What is the fewest weighings that always find both the heaviest and the lightest?

options.why: You found the heaviest in 9, then the lightest of the other 9 in 8. Weighing in pairs first shares the work.
That finds only one of them. The other needs more weighings.
That is one round of pairs. It leaves 5 candidates for each end.

feedback.correct: Pairs first (5), then the heaviest of the heavier five (4) and the lightest of the lighter five (4): 13.
feedback.generic: Weigh the parcels in pairs first. Only a heavier parcel of a pair can be the heaviest, and only a lighter one the lightest.

explain.text: Five weighings in pairs give 5 heavier and 5 lighter parcels. The heaviest is among the heavier five and the lightest among the lighter five, 4 weighings each, so 13. Fewer cannot work: 18 facts are needed, a loss for 9 parcels and a win for 9, and at most 5 weighings settle two at once.

items.title: A pooled test
items.question: Five samples are pooled and tested once. Each sample is positive with chance 0.1, independently, and the pool shows positive exactly when at least one is. The pool tests positive. What is the chance a given sample is positive? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: A positive sample always makes the pool positive, so divide its chance by the pool's.

byKey.one-in-five: You assumed the pool holds exactly one positive. Divide 0.1 by the chance the pool is positive.
byKey.pool: That is the chance the pool tests positive. You need one sample's chance given that.

explain.text: A positive sample makes the pool positive, so $P(\text{sample} \mid \text{pool}) = \tfrac{0.1}{P(\text{pool})}$. The pool is positive with chance $1 - 0.9^5 = 0.40951$, which gives $0.244$. Check: the pool holds 0.5 positives on average, or $\tfrac{0.5}{0.40951} \approx 1.221$ given it is positive, which is 0.244 per sample.

items.title: Until the dice drop
items.question: You roll a fair die again and again. You stop at the first roll that is lower than the roll before it. What is the expected number of rolls, the last one included?

options.why: That is $e$, the answer for draws that never tie. On a die, ties let the run go on.
You gave each roll an independent $\tfrac{5}{12}$ chance of dropping. After a high roll a drop is likelier.
You left out the final roll, the one that drops.

feedback.correct: The first $k$ rolls never drop with chance $\binom{k+5}{5} / 6^k$, and these chances add to $(\tfrac65)^6 \approx 2.99$.
feedback.generic: Let $m_j$ be the expected number of rolls still to come when the last roll was $j$. Condition on the next roll.

explain.text: With $m_j = 1 + \tfrac16 \sum_{i \ge j} m_i$, the top face gives $m_6 = \tfrac65$, and each face lower multiplies by $\tfrac65$, so $m_j = (\tfrac65)^{7 - j}$. The first roll then gives $1 + \tfrac16 \sum_j m_j = (\tfrac65)^6 \approx 2.99$. Check: the run lasts past $k$ rolls when they never fall, chance $\binom{k+5}{5} / 6^k$, and these add to $(1 - \tfrac16)^{-6}$.

items.title: Will the line die out
items.question: A trading idea spawns 0, 1 or 2 new ideas with chances $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac12$, and each new idea does the same, independently. What is the chance the line of ideas eventually dies out?

options.why: That is the chance the first idea has no offspring. Later generations can also die out.
You dropped the case of two new ideas, as if both their lines never die. That case dies out with chance $q^2$.
That is the chance it dies out within two generations. Later generations add more.

feedback.correct: Conditioning on the first idea, $q = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 q + \tfrac12 q^2$, with roots $\tfrac12$ and 1. The chance of dying out within $n$ generations climbs from 0 and stops at $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Let $q$ be the chance the line dies out. Each new idea's own line dies out with chance $q$, independently.

explain.text: Splitting on the first idea's offspring gives $q = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 q + \tfrac12 q^2$, so $2q^2 - 3q + 1 = 0$ and $q = \tfrac12$ or 1. The chance of dying out within $n$ generations follows $q_{n+1} = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 q_n + \tfrac12 q_n^2$ from $q_0 = 0$: $\tfrac14$, then $\tfrac{11}{32}$, and so on. A value below $\tfrac12$ always maps to one below $\tfrac12$, so the climb stops at $\tfrac12$, not 1.

items.title: Distance to the edge
items.question: A point lands uniformly at random in a square of side 1 metre. What is its expected distance to the nearest side, in metres? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: The distance exceeds $t$ with chance $(1 - 2t)^2$, which integrates to $\tfrac16$ over $0 \le t \le \tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Find $P(D > t)$: the point must lie in a central square of side $1 - 2t$.

byKey.one-way: That is the distance to the nearer of two opposite sides only. Take the nearest of all four.
byKey.centre: That is the centre's distance to a side, the farthest any point can be from every side.

explain.text: The point is more than $t$ from every side inside the central square of side $1 - 2t$, so $P(D > t) = (1 - 2t)^2$. Then $E[D] = \int_0^{1/2} (1 - 2t)^2 \, dt = \tfrac16 \approx 0.167$. Check: where the left side is nearest, $D = x$ on a strip of length $1 - 2x$, and $4 \int_0^{1/2} x(1 - 2x) \, dx = \tfrac16$.

items.title: Searching the same drawer
items.question: A missing trade ticket is in drawer A with chance 0.6, and otherwise in drawer B. Each search of drawer A finds the ticket, if it is there, with chance 0.8. You search A once and find nothing. What is the chance your next search of A finds it?

options.why: That ignores the failed search: $0.6 \times 0.8$.
That is the chance it is in A. The next search must also succeed.
That assumes the ticket is in A.

feedback.correct: After a miss it is in A with chance $\tfrac{0.12}{0.52} = \tfrac{3}{13}$, so the next search finds it with chance $\tfrac{3}{13} \times 0.8 = \tfrac{12}{65}$.
feedback.generic: First update the chance it is in A after one miss. The next search finds it only if it is there and the search works.

explain.text: A miss has chance $0.6 \times 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.52$, and leaves A with chance $\tfrac{0.12}{0.52} = \tfrac{3}{13}$. The next search finds it with chance $\tfrac{3}{13} \times 0.8 = \tfrac{12}{65} \approx 0.185$. Check: of 1,000 tickets, 120 in A and 400 in B are missed, and 96 of the 120 are found next, $\tfrac{96}{520}$.

items.title: A trader with desk-mates
items.question: At a firm, half the desks have 1 trader, 30% have 2 and 20% have 4. You meet a trader picked at random from the whole firm, and she has at least one desk-mate. What is the chance her desk has 4 traders? Give three decimal places.

feedback.correct: Traders at 4-trader desks weigh $0.2 \times 4 = 0.8$ against $0.3 \times 2 = 0.6$ at 2-trader desks, so $\tfrac{0.8}{1.4} = \tfrac47 \approx 0.571$.
feedback.generic: Picking a trader weights each desk by its size. Then drop the 1-trader desks.

byKey.desks: That is the share of shared desks with 4 traders. Big desks hold more of the traders.
byKey.no-clue: That weights desks by size but ignores the desk-mate news.
byKey.prior: That is the share of desks, not of traders.

explain.text: Desks average $0.5 + 0.6 + 0.8 = 1.9$ traders, so a random trader is at a 4-trader desk with chance $\tfrac{0.8}{1.9}$, a 2-trader desk with $\tfrac{0.6}{1.9}$. Having a desk-mate rules out the 1-trader desks, leaving $\tfrac{0.8}{0.6 + 0.8} = \tfrac47 \approx 0.571$. Check: 100 desks hold 190 traders, 140 have desk-mates and 80 of those sit at 4-trader desks.

items.title: How long the series runs
items.question: Two traders play a best-of-five series: the first to win 3 games wins it. Ann wins each game with chance 0.6, independently. What is the expected number of games played?

options.why: That is the answer for an even match. A stronger player ends the series sooner.
You assumed the series always runs to the fifth game.
You assumed one player sweeps. The series often needs more games.

feedback.generic: Find the chance the series ends after 3 games, after 4 and after 5.

explain.text: It ends at game 3 with chance $0.6^3 + 0.4^3 = 0.28$ and at game 4 with $3(0.6^3 \times 0.4 + 0.4^3 \times 0.6) = 0.3744$, leaving 0.3456 for game 5. So $E = 3 \times 0.28 + 4 \times 0.3744 + 5 \times 0.3456 = 4.0656$. Check: game 5 is played exactly when the first four split 2 to 2, chance $6 \times 0.36 \times 0.16 = 0.3456$.

items.title: Rolling for the point
items.question: You roll two fair dice. A total of 7 or 11 wins at once, and 2, 3 or 12 loses at once. Any other total becomes your point. You then roll until the point comes again, and win, or a 7 comes, and lose. What is the chance you win? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: A point that comes $w$ ways in 36 beats the 6 ways of a 7 with chance $\tfrac{w}{w + 6}$.

byKey.first-roll: That counts only the first-roll wins. Points are often won too.
byKey.even-race: You treated each point as an even race with 7. A 7 is likelier than any point.

explain.text: Points 4 and 10 come 3 ways in 36, 5 and 9 come 4 ways, and 6 and 8 come 5 ways. A point made $w$ ways beats the 6 ways of a 7 with chance $\tfrac{w}{w + 6}$, so you win with chance $\tfrac{8}{36} + 2(\tfrac{3}{36} \times \tfrac39 + \tfrac{4}{36} \times \tfrac{4}{10} + \tfrac{5}{36} \times \tfrac{5}{11}) = \tfrac{244}{495} \approx 0.493$. Check: the first roll wins $\tfrac{8}{36} = \tfrac{110}{495}$ and the points add $\tfrac{134}{495}$.

items.title: Rock, paper, scissors for four
items.question: Four traders play rock, paper, scissors together, each choosing at random. If exactly two of the three gestures appear, everyone showing the losing one is out; otherwise nobody is. Rounds go on until one trader is left. What is the expected number of rounds? Give three decimal places.

feedback.generic: Work up from two players: find the expected rounds with 2 left, then 3, then 4.

byKey.three: That is the answer for three players. Four need longer.
byKey.one-exit: You assumed each round removes one trader. A round can remove one, two or three.
byKey.two: That is the answer for two players.

explain.text: Two players settle a round with chance $\tfrac23$, so $E_2 = \tfrac32$, and the same first step gives $E_3 = \tfrac94$. With four, a round leaves 4, 3, 2 or 1 players in 39, 12, 18 and 12 of the 81 outcomes. So $\tfrac{42}{81} E_4 = 1 + \tfrac{18}{81} \times \tfrac32 + \tfrac{12}{81} \times \tfrac94 = \tfrac{135}{81}$, giving $E_4 = \tfrac{45}{14} \approx 3.214$.
